clue.text: 27 of 6s?

parts.note: the canines of the puzzle world: a breed of gundog shares its name with the people who compile puzzles

explanation.walkthrough: You need 27 (a set of hounds) and 6 (the puzzle on the page) first; the hounds that belong to puzzles are a gundog breed whose name also means puzzle compilers.
explanation.definitionFit: A gundog breed carries the same name as the compilers of puzzles, so puzzle people's hounds are those compilers.

clue.text: You translated poetry on the Sun

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece set on another comes after it

parts.note: sol is the Latin and French word for the sun
vers is French for verse, so poetry put into French

explanation.surface: Someone renders verse into another language while sitting in the sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You' is the definition: the clue speaks directly to the people doing the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The reader addressed as 'you' in a crossword is one of the people working out its clues.

clue.text: Fwightful cwimes without a subject of novel tale

indicators.note: without means the following letter is left out of the word

parts.note: frightful crimes are atrocities, here said with the R turned to W in a lisping baby-talk accent

explanation.surface: A baby-talk shudder at dreadful crimes, mixed up with the plot of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The W-for-R lisp turns atrocities into a word whose letters, less the A, name the two places in Dickens's novel of London and Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's novel about the French Revolution is set in London and Paris, the pair of places its title names.

clue.text: What happened to regular model?

parts.note: even means regular or uniform
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model gives T

explanation.surface: Someone asks what became of a dependable fashion model.
explanation.definitionFit: An occurrence is something that happened, so the phrase stands for that noun.

clue.text: Pole, old expert with ball, keeping it up, having an easy name?

parts.note: S is the south pole

indicators.note: keeping means holding the next piece inside

parts.note: Pele, the retired Brazilian footballer, was a famous expert with a ball

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A Polish veteran sportsman keeps a ball in the air, and has a name anyone can manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a nationality but is just a compass point; 'it' points back to the ball, which is the piece turned upwards. Pele was Brazil's great footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: A name that is easy is one people can write out letter by letter without trouble.

clue.text: Oath to the French king, one interrupting speech

parts.note: heck is a mild oath
le is French for the
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: An oath addressed to the King of France by someone shouting him down.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who shouts out to disrupt a speaker is the classic barracker at a meeting.

clue.text: Hard part of wader's cry to 9 "27 26"

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: only part of the bird's name is used, its last two letters dropped

parts.note: the avocet is a wading bird

explanation.surface: A tough bit of a wading bird's call, said to some quoted hounds.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Antony says Caesar's spirit will cry this word and let slip the hounds of battle; 9 gives LOOSE, 27 26 the quoted phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony's speech in Julius Caesar has the spirit shouting this word as the signal to unleash destruction.

clue.text: This could bar you from the Dunmow flitch

definitions.text: This could bar you from the Dunmow flitch

parts.words: This could bar you from the Dunmow flitch
parts.note: the Dunmow flitch, a side of bacon given at Great Dunmow in Essex, goes to a married couple who swear they have not quarrelled for a year and a day; one angry remark disqualifies them

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, an angry remark, and it would disqualify a couple; read as one, it is the puzzle itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A single angry exchange would disqualify a couple, while the joined-up word is the grid puzzle being solved.

clue.text: Girl to love catcher?

parts.note: a lass is a girl
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: A girl goes to her sweetheart, who catches her.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowboy's rope with a running noose is used to catch cattle and horses.

clue.text: Tory shambles containing rising of the people — top people

indicators.note: containing means holding the next piece inside
a shambles is a mess, so the letters are put into disorder
rising in a down clue means read upwards

parts.note: lay means of the people as opposed to the clergy

explanation.surface: A Conservative fiasco includes a popular uprising against the elite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shambles' muddles TORY into ROTY, which takes in YAL, LAY turned upwards by 'rising of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kings, queens and their families are the people at the very top of society.

clue.text: Free love — have no success without it

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: to lose is to have no success
love is nil in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Free love, but you will fail if you go without it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside, not lacking: LOSE goes round O.
explanation.definitionFit: To set free is to release, a synonym for the verb in the clue.

clue.text: You snivel unpleasantly, wishing you were me?

indicators.note: unpleasantly suggests the letters are twisted out of shape

explanation.surface: You whine nastily because you would like to be in my place.
explanation.definitionFit: Envy is wanting someone else's lot, so wishing to be another person is done in that resentful way.

clue.text: Put in letters for ice-breaker keeping weapon

indicators.note: keeping means holding the next piece inside
ice-breaker suggests the ice is broken into pieces and rearranged

parts.note: a pistol is a weapon

explanation.surface: A conversation opener carried in correspondence, with a gun tucked in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ice-breaker' looks like a social opener for a conversation, but only its second half does any work, scrambling the first half around the gun.
explanation.definitionFit: Epistles are letters, so something conveyed in correspondence is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Do this to cite this for 11

definitions.text: Do this to cite this for 11

indicators.note: the answer itself means to mess up, so it serves as the signal to rearrange the letters

parts.note: 11 across is the adjective meaning conveyed in letters

explanation.surface: An instruction telling you to wreck a word, with the wrecked word given as the result.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the answer's letters plus CITE, mixed together, make 11 across, EPISTOLIC, and the answer is also the verb that tells you to mix them.
explanation.definitionFit: To mar or ruin something is what the clue tells you to do to the letters of cite.

clue.text: Make music, including Western music

indicators.note: including means taking the next piece inside

parts.note: to sing is to make music

explanation.surface: A band plays, including some country and western numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: The big-band jazz style of the 1930s and 40s is a genre of popular dance music.

clue.text: Dormouse gets sulphur and oxygen on a sliding scale, perhaps

parts.note: Glis is the genus of the edible dormouse
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A dormouse is given two chemical elements and slides up a pay scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sliding scale' sounds like economics, but it means a run of notes slid up or down.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical slide runs up or down a scale, as when a finger sweeps across piano keys.

clue.text: Coster from Furness

definitions.meaning: a coster, short for costermonger, is a street seller of fruit and vegetables working from a handcart
a lad from the Cumbrian town of Barrow-in-Furness

explanation.walkthrough: Barrow-in-Furness is a shipbuilding town in Cumbria, so a young man from there fits the phrase, as does a London street trader with a cart.
explanation.definitionFit: A coster sells fruit from a handcart, so he is the street trader named for his cart.

clue.text: Quickly collected red coat and organised duel quietly

parts.note: rust is the reddish coating that forms on iron

indicators.note: organised means the letters are arranged into a new order

parts.note: P stands for piano, quietly in music

explanation.surface: A redcoat soldier calmly arranges a duel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red coat' suggests a British soldier, but it is the coat of rust; 'organised' rearranges DUEL as LEDU.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something together in a hurry, a meal or a team, is an idiom of improvising.

clue.text: From abbey to cathedral (almost) in Somerset — it's drier

parts.note: Bath Abbey is in the Somerset city of Bath

indicators.note: almost means the word stops short of its end

parts.note: Wells, in Somerset, is England's smallest cathedral city

explanation.surface: A journey between two Somerset landmarks ends with something to dry off with.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath and Wells are neighbouring places in Somerset; 'almost' cuts Wells to WEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A large absorbent cloth for drying the body after washing is a thing that dries.

clue.text: Ship's first come into old one's bell and pursued it with vigour

annotationWithheld.why: Ship's first come into old one's bell and pursued it with vigour: the parse is S into LUTINE plus SS, both from the one word Ship, so Ship does two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Ship's first come into old one's bell and pursued it with vigour

clue.text: Was stretched out on the ground, fatally wounded

definitions.text: Was stretched out on the ground

indicators.note: wounded suggests the word is damaged and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone lay sprawled on the ground after being mortally hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying stretched along the ground is the past of the phrasal verb meaning to lie level.

clue.text: Get rid of land on sea

definitions.meaning: to bring an aircraft down on water in an emergency

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to discard and to make an emergency landing of a plane on water.

clue.text: German one of 27 brings up, without colouring, time 26 between 1s (across and down)

parts.note: Hund is German for dog, one of the hounds in 27

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: rears means brings up, as a child
dye is a colouring

explanation.surface: A German hound rears young and spends a long time fighting between puzzle people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, not lacking. The first crossword appeared in 1913, so this 2013 puzzle marks a century of battle between compilers and solvers, echoing the long Anglo-French conflict.
explanation.definitionFit: A century is the span of time the famous Anglo-French medieval conflict was named after.

clue.text: See 20
Musical gunner in a pub raised a point

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means read upwards

parts.note: an inn is a pub
E is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: An artilleryman in a bar stands up to make a point.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical is Annie Get Your Gun, about the sharpshooter Annie Oakley.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irving Berlin show about the sharpshooter Oakley is often called by her first name alone.

clue.text: Supply lamps the ginnel needed …

indicators.note: needed sounds like kneaded, worked over like dough, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: An alleyway that has to be given lighting.
explanation.walkthrough: A ginnel is a northern English word for a narrow passage between houses.
explanation.definitionFit: To light something up, figuratively or literally, is to give it illumination.

clue.text: Wind once blowing from Europe to America?

parts.note: US is the United States

explanation.surface: An old wind blowing across the Atlantic from Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology the east wind was personified as this god, hence a wind of old.

clue.text: German/American artist given a little Polish money

definitions.meaning: George ..., the Berlin satirical painter who emigrated to the United States
a small Polish coin worth one hundredth of a zloty

explanation.definitionFit: The painter George shares his surname with the hundredth part of the Polish zloty.

clue.text: … needed again with heater fitted in Soviet city

parts.note: following the ellipsis, needed works on the ginnel of the clue before once more, giving a fresh arrangement of its letters
rad is short for radiator, a heater

explanation.surface: A Soviet city needed another heater installed.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the previous clue's ginnel over: 'needed again' rearranges those same six letters a second time, and the heater is fitted after them.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Petersburg bore Lenin's name during the Soviet era, from 1924 to 1991.

clue.text: See 27
Caesar's bulls forged? So what?

indicators.note: bulls as in nonsense, so the letters are made into rubbish; the bull was an emblem of Caesar's legions

explanation.surface: Were Caesar's bulls counterfeit? Who cares?
explanation.walkthrough: Antony in Julius Caesar says Caesar's spirit will 'let slip' these, the hounds of battle; 'bulls' is the anagram signal on FORGED and SO WHAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase belongs to Shakespeare's Caesar, whose vengeful spirit is pictured unleashing destruction through Antony's speech.

clue.text: Did the 6 — or was unable to?

definitions.meaning: worked at a crossword, 6 down, as a verb from the noun for a brainteaser
was baffled, unable to do it

explanation.walkthrough: The verb from the noun for a brainteaser means both tackling one and being baffled by it.
explanation.definitionFit: To work at a brainteaser and to be baffled by one share one past-tense word.
